connection: Session 20 created PayrollService with a clear foreach loop over completed entries. This session refactors that known behavior into LINQ and adds one small ordered-history query; it does not assume additional services or tests already exist.
objectives: Read a LINQ pipeline from source to result.
Use Where to keep completed entries and OrderByDescending to show newest entries first.
Use Sum with an inline projection to calculate total hours.
Create PayrollService with the interface dependency established in Session 20.

visuals.title: A query is a sequence of transformations
visuals.explanation: Source entries flow through filtering and ordering; each operator returns another sequence.

visuals.title: Where removes open entries
visuals.explanation: Only entries with a clock-out can safely provide a completed duration.

visuals.title: Sum projects and aggregates
visuals.explanation: The lambda converts each ClockEntry to hours; Sum combines those numbers into one total.

visuals.title: Ordering states a visible requirement
visuals.explanation: OrderByDescending on ClockIn produces newest-first history rather than relying on source insertion order.

preQuiz.prompt: Why filter open entries before calling GetDuration?
options: An open entry has no completed duration
preQuiz.explanation: The filter protects the duration invariant.

preQuiz.prompt: What does the lambda in Sum return?
options: The numeric hours for one entry
preQuiz.explanation: Sum projects each element to a number and aggregates those numbers.

preQuiz.prompt: Does OrderByDescending modify the source collection?
options: No; it returns an ordered sequence
preQuiz.explanation: LINQ query operators do not reorder the original List.

concept.title: Where filters by a requirement
paragraphs: A completed-history query excludes entries whose clock-out is null before any duration calculation.
Use the Clockout/ClockOut spelling present in your current ClockEntry class.

concept.title: Sum can project and aggregate
paragraphs: PayrollService obtains completed entries through IClockEntryRepository, then maps each one to GetDuration().TotalHours inside Sum.
There is no need for a separate Select when no caller needs the intermediate sequence of numbers.

concept.title: Ordering should express the caller's need
paragraphs: CompletedNewestFirst uses OrderByDescending because a history screen normally shows recent entries first.
The returned IEnumerable remains a query; Session 23 examines when it actually executes.

lab.objective: Refactor the Session 20 total-hours loop to Sum and create one query that filters completed entries and orders them newest first.
lab.startingCondition: IClockEntryRepository and ClockEntryService exist. PayrollService and ClockEntryQueries do not exist yet.
steps: Create PayrollService.cs in the Domain project.
Declare a public sealed PayrollService class.
Inject IClockEntryRepository through its constructor using the Session 20 pattern.
Stub CalculateTotalHours with employeeId, startDate, and endDate parameters.
Return Sum with a lambda that projects each entry to GetDuration().TotalHours.
Build before adding the second query.
Create ClockEntryQueries.cs in the Domain project.
Declare a public static ClockEntryQueries class.
Stub CompletedNewestFirst with an IEnumerable<ClockEntry> parameter.
Filter to completed entries using the clock-out property in your source.
Order the result by ClockIn descending.
Return the pipeline without calling ToList.
Append a Session 21 section to App and display the total and ordered ClockIn values.

steps.text: Run App, then build and test. Compare with the solution after attempting both queries.
steps.code:
dotnet run --project src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.App.csproj --configuration Release
dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: Match GetDuration and Clockout/ClockOut to your existing ClockEntry API.

lab.expectedBehavior: Production uses LINQ to express existing filtering and ordering requirements without adding a second fictional feature.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Create total-hours behavior when LINQ provides its implementation.
Align the LINQ lesson with real prerequisites.

commit: session-21: teach linq filtering projection and ordering
review: The lab uses production because that is the most natural environment for this concept.
Every referenced application artifact was created in this session or an earlier session.
Earlier production code, tests, and ScratchPad experiments remain intact.

postQuiz.prompt: Why can Sum contain entry => entry.GetDuration().TotalHours?
options: Sum accepts a selector that produces the number to add
postQuiz.explanation: Projection and aggregation can be combined when the intermediate values are not needed.

postQuiz.prompt: Why does CompletedNewestFirst not call ToList?
options: The caller has not requested a snapshot
postQuiz.explanation: Session 23 will make the execution-time choice explicit.

postQuiz.prompt: What changes if OrderBy is used instead of OrderByDescending?

reflections: Which requirement does each LINQ operator represent?
When would a separate Select make the intermediate values clearer?
Why should open-entry filtering happen before duration calculation?
whatBreaks: Removing the completed-entry filter allows an open entry into code that calls GetDuration and can trigger an exception. Reversing OrderByDescending changes newest-first history to oldest-first. Adding ToList here would force materialization before Session 23 explains that choice.
summary: Session 21 refactors a known foreach total into Sum and adds one completed, newest-first query. Every operator serves a visible requirement, and the lesson uses the ClockEntry member names present in the learner's source.
